newsitem.title: CHINA: China car market seen moving towards small, cheap.
newsitem.headline: China car market seen moving towards small, cheap.

text.p: U.S. car giant General Motors on Thursday formally started work on its huge Shanghai plant to make mid-sized sedans, but industry officials said the future of China's market would lie with smaller, cheaper cars.

General Motors (GM) has lauded the future car complex, which will cover 600,000 square metres (720,000 square yards), as a huge step toward winning over an automobile market that industry analysts say will eventually be one of the world's biggest.
GM officials at the official ground-breaking of the factory proudly showed off the 2.98-litre mid-sized Buick Regal sedan that the plant will produce when it goes on line in April 1999.
"Part of the reason GM decided to make a Buick-sized car at the Buick price range is because only institutions can buy now," said one GM official who declined to be identified.

Government agencies and corporations now make up the bulk of passenger car purchases, but industry officials are predicting a revolution in Chinese purchasing patterns within 10-15 years as Beijing moves to bolster the auto sector.

"China cannot rely wholly on institutional buyers to develop the automobile industry," said Xia Fang, a sales official with Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp, which has a 50 percent stake in the GM venture.

Demand for private cars would become a major force in the market within 10-15 years as more of China's 1.2 billion people became richer, Xia said, adding that models now made in China would be too pricey for the average family.
"If we want to develop a family car it must be a smaller car," he said.
Japan's Honda Motor Co Ltd has also forecast compact cars would become a mainstay of China's auto sector, saying it would like to market its Civic model there.
China produced about 384,000 cars last year and would make 450,000 units this year, said Eric Carlson, sales manager for Volkswagen Asia-Pacific.
"People are car-crazy here, no doubt about it," Carlson said in an interview. "They can't necessarily afford a family car yet but buying a car is something everyone aspires to."

But the Chinese government will need to remove barriers to private ownership such as exorbitant licence fees, and develop a system of consumer credit to facilitate personal car purchases, Carlson said.
To feed that institutional appetite -- which officials said accounted for up to 95 percent of China's car purchases -- output at GM's factory is to reach 100,000 units by early next century.

GM officials said Beijing had not promised to buy a fixed number of the Buicks and would leave the cars to compete against domestically-produced Volkswagen Santanas and Audis, as well as with imports such as Mercedes and BMWs.
"Government agencies would be potential customers, but there have been no guarantees," said Ian Stones, managing director of General Motors Asia.
Both GM and Volkswagen are also sinking money into research and development centres in China that would be essential to gain official Chinese favour and market share, officials said.

"Its prime function is to develop vehicle design capability in China," said one GM official of the $50 million Pan-Asia Technical Automotive Centre Ltd that GM is operating as a separate joint venture with Shanghai Automotive.
Volkswagen last month opened a $120 million proving ground that it said would give its Shanghai joint venture the power to develop its own cars.
The new GM and Volkswagen facilities are sure to please China's industry mandarins, who have stressed the importance of technology transfer and training to potential foreign business partners.
"You can't simply take a Western design and give it to the Chinese," Volkswagen's Carlson said. "You certainly can't take yesterday's design."
